newsitem.title: USA: NYC Giuliani praises state's new budget pact.
newsitem.headline: NYC Giuliani praises state's new budget pact.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has had a stormy relationship with Governor George Pataki, went out of his way to praise the governor for treating the city fairly in the new state's budget pact.
Pataki, in turn, applauded the mayor's efforts, at a joint news briefing. Both are Republicans.

New York City's mayor said "I can't think of a time in which the City of New York has come out better in terms of realistic things we need and that we can do in partnership with the state to help the people in the city."

Giuiliani pointed to big increases in state spending on education and changes in the welfare system. A $2.4 billion school bond act will be on November's ballot, and New York State will raise school aid by $750 million.

The state also will pay for a 10-percent cut in the city's personal income tax to help make sure its residents are not left out of a four-year, $2.2 billion property tax cut. New York City, unlike other localities in the state, pays for its schools with a variety of taxes, not just property taxes.

The state's new pact only gives the city $35 million for back school claims, though it is owed up to $900 million. Pataki said the payment would take care of most of the claims run up under his tenure, adding he wanted to phase-in payments of older claims.
Pataki applauded Giuliani for cutting violent crime, reducing welfare rolls and pushing Albany's lawmakers not to make the state's welfare system more costly.

"When I talk about New York State leading the nation, the person who has worked so hard to make workfare a success in the city, the person whose leadership has led the city to the most dramatic decline in violent crime in history, I believe, is Mayor Guiliani," said Pataki.

The governor, who said he and Giuliani both would have preferred to partly end this year clothing sales taxes on items that cost less than $100, added he hoped many counties would match the two, one-week breaks that were agreed for fiscal 1998. The state's new fiscal year started April 1, and the state's budget, which likely will not be finalized until over the weekend, is 121 days late.

Asked if a move by New York City to match the state's sales tax breaks would hurt surrounding counties, which may lose retail customers, Pataki replied they would benefit from the state's success in reducing welfare rolls and its plans to cut Medicaid costs by shifting recipients to managed care.
The state will not end its four-percent tax on items of clothing that cost less than $100 until 1999.
